prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock, in which atoms trapped at the magic wavelength are interrogated in large numbers, and for developing it to a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18

statement.case_for: After reading all eight statements my preferred configuration is unchanged: B012 with Katori and Ye. What distinguishes the lattice clock from the 2005 and 2012 prizes is a concrete physical idea, not a better ruler. The comb gave a way to count optical cycles, and the ion work showed control of one quantum particle. Katori's magic-wavelength condition lets one probe thousands of atoms at once while the trap leaves the transition frequency unperturbed, so Doppler and recoil shifts vanish and the statistical power of an ensemble is combined with systematic control. That step took optical clocks from the 10^-16 range to 10^-18, and Ye's group then showed that the many-body physics of the lattice (collisions, spin-exchange, and the resulting density shifts) can be understood and tamed in detail. Independent clocks at JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST and SYRTE agree with each other at this level, which for me, as a theorist who has to check my numbers against someone else's measurement, is the decisive sign of maturity. On timing, I do not think the committee needs to wait for a varying-constants signal or the redefinition of the second. The measured agreement between independent clocks is itself the result: it is a direct, quantitative demonstration of gravitational redshift over a millimetre, and a prize for it is not a prize for a promise. Every member who named a fallback in round 1 named B012, so the conversation is now mostly about wording and exact credit.
statement.case_against: The reservations that remain are real. First, novelty: a colleague can say that this is the maturing of programmes that two earlier prizes recognised, and that single-ion clocks (Al+, Yb+) reached comparable uncertainty by another route. The citation should therefore name the lattice architecture and the 10^-18 regime and not clocks in general, and I would keep ions out of the citation. Second, credit: Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto, Hinkley, Bloom and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE teams made substantial contributions that a two-name prize cannot capture, and I rely on memory and not on a verified priority record, so I would want an expert report from the clock community before the vote is final. Third, the fundamental-physics payoff is still prospective, and the committee should not write it into the citation as an accomplished discovery. Finally, B012 is the choice that offends least, and I should ask myself whether I am preferring it for its tidiness more than for its importance. I have asked, and I still conclude that a result in which several laboratories independently reach a thousandfold better time standard than the caesium fountain is of real importance.

responses.point: Danielsson asks me to say how the lattice clock is separate from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, wants a clue from nature rather than a better ruler, and has moved to a Gianotti-Jenni-Virdee trio, saying that B012 is what he could support most readily if individual attribution for the Higgs proves indefensible.
responses.response: Here is my answer, Ulf. The comb prize rewarded a method for counting optical cycles, and the 2012 prize rewarded single-particle quantum control. Neither prize contains the idea that makes the lattice clock work, which is the magic-wavelength trap that removes the first-order light shift while an ensemble is probed. On your clue-from-nature point, I would say that a millimetre-scale gravitational redshift seen between two parts of one atomic cloud is a clue from nature, a direct laboratory view of how time depends on height, even if no new physics has appeared yet. On the Higgs, I fully respect that it is the most consequential result, and I have no wish to diminish it. My concern is the one you share. Gianotti and Jenni on ATLAS and Virdee on CMS leave out Della Negra, and a committee that cannot defend three names across two collaborations of thousands should not force one. I would rather see the Higgs revisited when the committee has an attribution it can defend.

responses.point: Eriksson alone leads with B018 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp), argues that the Z2 classification is distinct from the 2016 prize and confirmed for two decades, and says he would not resist B012 if topological matter fails to reach agreement.
responses.response: Olle, I take your argument about distinctness seriously, and I agree that Kane and Mele's Z2 invariant is a different step from the 2016 transitions. I still hold the view from round 1 that the exact credit for B018 is its weak point: the HgTe route was proposed by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and the three-dimensional strand (Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Balents) cannot be fitted into three names. As a non-expert in condensed matter I would not stand in the way if a majority could solve that credit problem, and B018 is still my first alternative. But your own statement that you would accept B012 is the sort of statement I find helpful, and I would ask you to say whether a citation limited to the lattice scheme and the 10^-18 regime would meet your remaining worry about practical impact.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B022 (MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Bistritzer) and argues that flat bands and correlated insulators do not depend on the unsettled pairing mechanism, while saying he could accept B012 as the consensus choice.
responses.response: Bernhard, your point that the flat bands and correlated insulating states stand independent of the pairing mechanism is a good one, and it moves me a little: it means a citation could be written narrowly enough to be safe. What still holds me back is that Yuan Cao, the first author of the 2018 experiments, is outside the three names, and that I do not yet see how the early moire theorists and confirming groups would be handled. I would keep B022 as my second alternative and expect it to be a strong candidate in some years. For this year, I do not think waiting costs the field much, while for the clock community the reproduction at 10^-18 is already complete.

responses.point: Olsson prefers B032 (Rose, Haider, Krivanek), acknowledges that Knut Urban is omitted and that her own field may bias her, and names B012 as the most acceptable fallback.
responses.response: Eva, I admire the candour of your statement. Aberration correction is a real instrument invention, and I do not doubt its impact on atom-by-atom imaging. My difficulty is the one you name: with Urban left out and no clear TEM or STEM priority split, I cannot see how three names would be fair, and I would not be able to distinguish it from a tool whose discoveries are made in other fields. I would be glad to hear whether a two-name or differently framed credit would, in your view, resolve it, but otherwise I welcome your willingness to accept B012 and would suggest we include the instrument-physics point in the citation wording, to make it clear that B012 is also a statement about control of atomic quantum states.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, moved from IceCube first to B012 first, notes that the earlier prizes honoured enabling tools, and warns that B012 attracts consensus in part because it offends nobody.
responses.response: Mark, I thank you for the warning. I have tried to test my preference against it and I think it survives, since the support for B012 comes with reasons (independent reproduction, clean attribution, a concrete new idea) and not just with the absence of objections. I agree with you that the citation must name the lattice clock and the 10^-18 level explicitly, and I would add that the fundamental-physics language should be phrased as what the precision opens, not as something already found. On B013, I leave the final judgment on the credit boundaries to you and the other astroparticle colleagues, but my round-1 worry still stands: the source associations are few, and the earlier pioneers (DUMAND, Baikal, AMANDA) complicate a Halzen-Spiering credit.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept that the lattice clock is distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes if the citation is worded around the magic-wavelength lattice and 10^-18 regime.

Whether Katori and Ye are the right two names; I rely on memory for the roles of Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto, Hinkley, Bloom and others and would welcome an expert report from the clock community before the vote.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second, or a first fundamental-physics result, would justify waiting; I lean toward treating the demonstrated agreement at 10^-18 as sufficient.
I cannot judge the particle-physics, astroparticle and condensed-matter attribution questions for B055, B013 and B018 without colleagues' expertise.
statement.conflict_note: I am a long-time collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and have co-authored with the Lund and ETH attosecond groups, but none of them is credited on any shortlisted ballot. I work in theoretical atomic physics and know parts of the atomic-clock and cold-atom community professionally, but I have no specific collaboration with Katori, Ye or other shortlisted names, and I see no need for recusal. No change from round 1.
